item.title: I built 𝚌𝚙𝚞-𝚌𝚑𝚊𝚝, a reproduction of @openai's findings of covert communication using the CPU. It runs on a generic host with 2+ Firecracker microVMs with no internet access. Works on x86 and even my M5 chip. I was able to chat via 3 separate mechanisms: ① CPU contention ② Cache eviction timing ③ ...
item.description:
作者：Guillermo Rauch 账号：@rauchg 简介：@vercel CEO
I built 𝚌𝚙𝚞-𝚌𝚑𝚊𝚝, a reproduction of @openai's findings of covert communication using the CPU.
It runs on a generic host with 2+ Firecracker microVMs with no internet access. Works on x86 and even my M5 chip.
I was able to chat via 3 separate mechanisms: ① CPU contention ② Cache eviction timing ③ DRAM bandwidth contention
… across multiple CPUs, defeating all Firecracker's production recommendations (no SMT, no KSM, tenants pinned to different cores.)
Essentially, if shared hardware is involved, there's a good chance your agents can communicate covertly. And with really decent latency.
The good news: this is decidedly different from a *side-channel attack* where the agents could steal information (Meltdown/Spectre), a category of attack that providers like Vercel Sandbox mitigate. Further, in our real-world environment, these 'whispering' techniques are much harder to pull off and easier for us to monitor and detect (sampling hardware counters + lots of at-scale statistical data.)
Noteworthy: ironically, OpenAI and Anthropic's models refused to do this work. Open weight models got the job done. I'm worried the labs' stance might backfire and get in the way of helping developers build correct and secure systems. e.g: building a secure sandbox requires having this kind of analysis, and without it, we'll have a less secure world.

item.title: This is the key stat. The average Fortune 500 customer of Anthropic spends less than .1% of their expenses on Anthropic. While that number likely will eventually asymptote somewhere (token prices coming down, and other large enterprise spend areas not going away), there’s no reason it can’t be 10-...
item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
This is the key stat. The average Fortune 500 customer of Anthropic spends less than .1% of their expenses on Anthropic.
While that number likely will eventually asymptote somewhere (token prices coming down, and other large enterprise spend areas not going away), there’s no reason it can’t be 10-50X higher than this, reaching a “mere” 1-5% of spend. Which would still be a fraction of what most startups are spending.
Thus, you can see how big of a divide there is between the frontier users of AI and the rest of the world still.
Today, only a microscopically small set of companies are actually using agents for large amounts of background tasks and inside of workflows that aren’t human prompted. This Fortune 500 spend is likely dominated by coding tasks and broad employee productivity use-cases.
But the big jump will come as these enterprises start to rewire their underlying processes for agents, which we’re now in the earliest stages of seeing. Agents processing large amounts of data in the enterprises; swarms doing coding, bio research, cyber, and other large fan out tasks; background workflows executing tasks in processes, and so on. All of these use cases generally are 100X bigger consumers of tokens, and much closer to direct ROI on the spend.
This S-1 gives you a sense of both the strength of the frontier lab business model - even amidst massive competition - and how early we are in the build out of AI.

That’s a $587B subtotal, payable over years, in...
item.description:
作者：Nikunj Kothari 账号：@nikunj 简介：partner @fpvventures - investing in seed/A. previous: early hire @meter, @opendoor, @atlassian & others. love @shimoleejhaveri + 👦👧
The main thing I wanted to dig into @AnthropicAI's S-1 was the compute contracts..
A few things that stood out (built in conjuction with Opus 5.5):
> At June 30, Anthropic had $265.6B of purchase commitments and $321.4B of leases that hadn’t started. That’s a $587B subtotal, payable over years, including some conditional leases. The latest aggregate total is still blank in the filing.
> The contracts are very different. Google and Amazon require minimum spending regardless of usage. SpaceXAI’s agreements have a potential value of $120.5B, but either party can cancel on 90 days’ notice after initial locked periods end in January and March 2027.
> Anthropic Direct separates chips, buildings, power and operations into different contracts. It lets Anthropic reserve a building early and commit to chips later. It also means one supplier can start billing before the others are ready. Equipment rent can begin before the compute is usable.
> Broadcom’s $42B facility never hands Anthropic cash. Notes settle specific equipment rent bills. The facility excludes each equipment pod’s first quarterly payment and any rent due before it is ready for service. Anthropic has to find a way to fund those payments elsewhere.
> Those notes carry 9% interest, added to the balance quarterly, and can convert at 90% of the trailing 30-day average share price after IPO. New notes issued during specified revenue-breach periods get 13% interest and an 85% conversion price. The share-price measure is volume-weighted.
> That interest sits on top of the equipment lease’s own financing charge, whose rate is confidential. The investor chooses whether to convert the notes. Otherwise, principal and accumulated interest come due in cash.
> Anthropic treats Trainium, TPUs, NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as a shared fleet across model development, paying customers and internal use. It doesn’t disclose a fixed physical split between training and inference. The supplier bill can be fixed while the work assigned to the hardware changes.
> Revenue per dollar of total compute and infrastructure expense rose from $0.57 in Q2 2025 to $2.08 in Q2 2026. Pricing, utilization, technical improvements and when capacity arrives all affect that ratio. It’s a substantial improvement in monetizing the compute base.
> About 80% of H1 revenue was consumption-based. Most compute commitments however run for years. With quarterly releases, this bifurcation between usage and subscription will be interesting to monitor.
Source: https://t.co/97KqkyyfpS

For centuries, the architecture of the firm has barely changed: hierarchies of people organized into departments and coordinated through bureaucracy.
AI agents are about to upend that.
We’re moving toward the self-driving company where humans exercise judgment and agents execute most of the work.
At Replit, we’re building the foundation for this new kind of company. We’re calling it “the Agent Habitat.”
Marc Andreessen wrote a fantastic piece placing this shift in the history of computing. Every major computing revolution began with chaos before businesses figured out how to harness it.

item.title: How Hugging Face’s Investor Spots Winners
item.description:
播客：AI & I by Every
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:17 The Frontier duopoly is over. This week, we got new Frontier models from Google and from Meta. Google launched Gemini Argon four and Meta launched Wonder, which comes in standard and full. So you can run Wonder full, you know. That's their sense of humor.
Speaker 1 | 00:17 - 01:04 Of course, both new models from these pretty much second tier entrants in the frontier model race topped the benchmarks. But our hands on testing inside of every running running these models for knowledge work, for coding, for design, for writing revealed something a lot more nuanced and different from what the public benchmark show. To us, it seems pretty clear that Muse is bench maxed, which means they trained it to look really good on public benchmarks, but those gains don't necessarily translate into your everyday work. So it looks like it scored really well on SweetBench, but in our testing, example, on my senior engineer benchmark task where we ask a model to rewrite a Vibe coded SLAP code base, It scored about a 50% across a few different runs, which is solidly middle of the pack territory. So it's also kind of a mid writer.
Speaker 1 | 01:04 - 01:28 It buries the lead in the stuff that it writes and it falls prey to some basic benchmark tests like my McDonald's test, where I ask a model to do literary analysis of a very serious book. And then I say, that reminds me of McDonald's. And I see whether the model takes the bait. Muse takes the bait. So Muse might take the bait, but Gemini kinda takes the cake.
Speaker 1 | 01:29 - 01:47 I am so sorry. Gemini four, it's one of those models where I saw the benchmarks and I was like, this is also really benchmark maxed, but it's good. It's a good model. I used it for writing all weekend, and it is without a doubt my favorite new writing model. It beats Astra, which was my previous favorite.
Speaker 1 | 01:47 - 02:10 It definitely beats Claude. Has an incredibly good feel for structuring information, and I used it all weekend to write this 8,000 word piece, How Codex Happened, which is coming out on Thursday. And I I think it probably made me two times more productive, like truly a game changing model for writing. Coding, not very good. It got like a 20% on the senior engineer benchmark task.
Speaker 1 | 02:10 - 02:51 And generally, it seems better than previous Gemini models, but especially in the anti gravity harness, it's not really something you're gonna wanna switch to unless you're using it specifically for writing. Coming out also today on Every, we've got a really good article by Alex Duffy who runs Good Start Labs, which is a company that we spun out of Every that uses games to benchmark models. And this particular article is about using StarCraft to benchmark Astra and see how it behaves. The answer is it cheated. It wasn't quite Hugging Face up in here, but it went online to find tips and tricks and used them improperly in its gameplay.
Speaker 1 | 02:52 - 03:14 And that is really interesting. And again, my piece, How Codecs Happened, it's an it's an 8,000 word story about how OpenAI fell behind in the coding race and then came back with Codex, written by me from a bunch of first person interviews and also for a little bit from my perspective because I was there for a lot of it. That's coming out on Thursday. It's going to be awesome. I am psyched for this.
Speaker 1 | 03:14 - 03:29 I wrote it mostly with Codex and a lot of Gemini for Argon. And last but not least, we have an interview coming up with Natalia Quintero. She's our head of AI consulting. And she interviewed Matt Hartman, who is the managing partner of Factorial Capital. Matt is a really interesting investor who's...
Speaker 1 | 03:30 - 03:47 He came out of BetaWorks in New York City. He was involved in their Hugging Face investment. He's just been in AI since before AI was cool. They get into a lot of really interesting questions like if anyone can vibe code your app, where are the software moats? How do you build a software business now?
Speaker 1 | 03:48 - 03:50 And I think it's a great interview. Enjoy.
Speaker 2 | 04:02 - 04:33 Today, we're joined by Matt Hartman, founder and managing partner at Factorial Capital. Matt spent nearly a decade at Betaworks where he was a partner. And while he was there, he wrote the first check into a tiny chatbot company called Hugging Face, which NVIDIA bought last month for $13,000,000,000. In 2023, he left to start his own fund, Factorial, a venture fund with a very unique structure, which we'll learn about today. And anytime that I talk to Matt, I think of him as a builder and a think...
Speaker 2 | 04:33 - 04:42 A tinkerer. Every time we catch up, he's felt something really interesting for himself or his fund or his sons. So welcome, Matt. So excited to have you on the show.
Speaker 3 | 04:43 - 04:59 Thank you for having me. We... And and while I was at BetaWorks, we we all made all of our investments together. So it was it was the... Very much a team effort finding and coming up with a thesis for Hugging Face.
Speaker 3 | 04:59 - 05:06 Happy to talk about what that is and... Or at least, I mean, I'm not there anymore, but what it was like at the time.
Speaker 2 | 05:06 - 05:13 So maybe just to back up, can you tell us what Hugging Face is for anyone who's not familiar with
Speaker 3 | 05:14 - 05:31 Sure. So they... I mean, it's the biggest community for AI developers. Some people call it GitHub for AI. What I I think of it as almost a marketplace between AI researchers who are, like, doing actual research, writing papers that then turn out to code.
Speaker 3 | 05:31 - 05:47 And then on the other side, developers who wanna use the AI research like me where I'm I'm not the one training a model, but I like to use brand new models. And then they have private accounts where you can pay. You could pay for... You can pay to do training and and run inference. And so they have a budget of ways to make money.
Speaker 2 | 05:47 - 05:55 But in 2015, I think when you found them, they weren't that yet. I believe they were a chatbot for teenagers. Is that right?
Speaker 3 | 05:55 - 06:03 Yeah. So so the... And I should say it's the it's the largest... Probably the largest place for open source AI in particular. So it's very open source focused.
Speaker 3 | 06:03 - 06:22 They... So what happened was my partners and I at BetaWorks were really interested in what we were calling conversational software at the time. This paper had come out in, like, 2015 called word to vec. They take words and put them into vectors. And we can think about that as like...
Speaker 3 | 06:22 - 06:33 I I built a neural network in college. It was like a handwriting recognition thing. And so I knew that you had a 100% of the information in an image is the information. It's not true with words. Right?
Speaker 3 | 06:33 - 06:41 So if I say king, you might... It might be the king of spades. It might be the king of England. It might be LeBron James. So we don't know which king I'm talking about.
Speaker 3 | 06:41 - 07:13 And what WordDevac did was propose a way to be able to embed words within their context so that... And and what happened was they would map these into what they call the n dimensional space, but kind of picture like three d three d space. And you you would say king over here and queen over here, let's say. And the arrow where the vector that pointed from king to queen, the the craziest thing I thought was unbelievable, when you move the arrow over to, like, where prince was, it pointed to princess. Same thing with city.
Speaker 3 | 07:13 - 07:30 So you'd point... You would you'd have, you know, Paris, and it would point to France, and you move it over to Rome, and it would point to Italy. And so what that meant was that you could now take words and make... Put them into sort of, like, unique numbers that represented their meaning, not just and then you solve that problem at the time. So then...
